name: Maasai
era: From about the 15th century to today
line: Greet everyone with respect, walk your land, look after what is in your care and give when you are asked.

quote.text: One finger does not kill a louse.
quote.source: Recorded by A. C. Hollis in The Masai: Their Language and Folklore, 1905. Nothing is done alone

quotes.text: The neck cannot go above the head.
quotes.source: On the respect owed to those who are older; in Naomi Kipury, Oral Literature of the Maasai, 1983

quotes.text: The eye that has travelled is wise.
quotes.source: A common English rendering. One who has seen other places understands more

quotes.text: Mountains do not meet, but people do.
quotes.source: Shared with other peoples of East Africa. Said at partings, and to those who quarrel

quotes.text: God, give us children and cattle.
quotes.source: The usual petition of morning prayers and blessings, in a common English rendering

quotes.text: A zebra does not despise its stripes.
quotes.source: Widely quoted as Maasai; the original Maa form is not given in the sources consulted

words.usage: Maasai means the people who speak Maa. It is a Nilotic language, related to those of the upper Nile, and is shared with the Samburu and others.
One God. The word is grammatically feminine. Enkai is called the Black God when kind, like a rain cloud, and the Red God when angry, like the dry season.
The first virtue. It means honour, obedience to elders, modesty and good manners, and it governs how every age and sex behaves toward the others.
A lifelong partnership in which each gives to the other in real need, with no debt recorded and no repayment expected.
The fullness of life that elders ask for in blessing: many children, many cattle, peace and old age.
The centre of Maasai life. Food, wealth, bride-gift, fine and sacrifice. Tradition says Enkai sent them down from the sky for the Maasai to keep.
Each animal is known by its colour, horn shape, temper and line of descent, and many have names.
The management of livestock, pasture and water. The same word covers looking after people and land.
Several families’ houses in a ring inside a thorn fence, with the cattle brought into the middle at night.
Low and loaf-shaped, built by the women from a frame of poles plastered with mud and cattle dung. A house belongs to the woman who built it.
A camp built for an age-set of young men, where they live apart with their mothers and learn to govern themselves.
All the men initiated in the same period of about fifteen years. They move through life together and are equals for good.
A young man of the junior age grade, charged with protecting people and herds. The plural is ilmurran.
A married man who has left warriorhood. Elders hold authority, settle disputes and give blessings.
Chosen for good sense and fair speech. He leads discussion and speaks for his fellows, and cannot give orders.
A man of one particular family who divines, makes medicines and advises on ceremonies. Outsiders called him the laibon.
Matters are settled by talk under a tree, where each man may speak in turn until agreement is reached.
One of the sixteen or so divisions of the Maasai, each with its own land and age-sets, such as the Purko, Kisongo and Loita.
Held in common by a section. Families moved over it with the seasons, resting pasture as they went.
One word for both. Almost every plant of the savanna has a use that herders learn as children.
A sacred tree, linked with Enkai. People pray and make offerings beneath it.
The daily food, drunk fresh or soured from a long gourd cleaned with a burning stick of wild olive.
A place in the bush where men withdraw to slaughter an animal, eat, rest and gather strength, with soups made from bark and roots.
Warriors take turns to leap straight up from a standing start, heels never touching the ground, while the others sing.

words.meaning: The cloth worn as a wrap
words.usage: Usually red, often checked. Known across East Africa by the Swahili word shuka.
A short wooden club with a knob, carried by men. A black one is the sign of an elder or a leader.
The greeting to a man. The answer is ipa. A woman is greeted with takwenya and answers iko.
Ashe alone is thank you.
Said on parting.
The Maasai name for the years 1883 to 1902, when cattle plague, smallpox and drought killed most of their herds and a great many people.

practices.name: Greet with respect
practices.instructions: Greet every person you meet this morning, and take your time over it. Stop, look at them and ask how they are, and then how their family is. Let them answer. Greet older people first and let them speak first. With those you live or work with, do not begin on any business until the greetings are finished. Thank people aloud and say goodbye when you leave.
practices.why: Respect, enkanyit, is the first Maasai virtue, and greeting is where it shows. Greetings are long and ask after the home, the children and the cattle. A child greets an elder by bowing the head to be touched. To pass someone without greeting is an insult.
variations: Learn the greetings in Maa: supa and ipa, takwenya and iko.
Ring an older relative only to ask how they are.
Greet a neighbour you have never spoken to.

practices.name: Walk your land
practices.instructions: Walk for forty minutes at a steady pace through the place where you live, without headphones. Walk as a herder walks: upright, unhurried, looking far ahead. Notice the state of things. Where is the water. What is growing and what is dry. Which way the wind is blowing and what the sky is doing. Who is about. Learn the name of one plant, bird or place you pass.
practices.why: Herding is walking. A herder may cover twenty kilometres in a day, and boys begin with the calves and goats at about five. The work depends on knowing every stretch of pasture, each water point, the uses of the plants and the signs of the weather. Land was rested by moving on.
variations: Carry a stick, as every herder does.
Walk the same route each week and note what has changed.
Find out where your water comes from.

practices.name: Count what is in your care
practices.instructions: Name the living things and the people that depend on you: children, parents, animals, plants, a team, a friend in trouble. Go to each one today, in person if you can, and look at them properly. Is this one well. Has it eaten. Is anything wrong that you had not noticed. Do the one thing that most needs doing, before you do anything for yourself.
practices.why: A herder knows each animal in a herd of hundreds by its colour, its horns and its mother, and sees at once if one is missing or sick. Wealth is counted in what is alive and in your keeping. Maasai tradition holds that cattle were entrusted to them by Enkai, which makes the keeping a duty.
variations: Check on someone in your care by going to see them.
Look after a plant or an animal daily for the month.
Find out which cattle breeds are kept where you live, and by whom.

practices.name: Give when you are asked
practices.instructions: If someone asks you today for something they really need, give it if you can, and give no more than is needed. Do not write it down. Do not mention it again or expect it back. If nobody asks, think of one person with whom you could have this kind of bond, and one real need of your own that you have been too proud to ask help with. Ask.
practices.why: Maasai herders form partnerships called osotua, a word that also means the umbilical cord. A partner who is in real need may ask, and the other must give what he can spare. No debt is created and no account is kept, and the tie passes down to the children. Studies of the system show that it protects whole communities from drought.
variations: Ask a friend for help with one real need.
Find out how neighbours near you share in hard times.

practices.name: Talk it through at the fire
practices.instructions: Sit down with the people you live with when the day’s work is over, around a fire, a candle or the table. Let the oldest speak first. If there is a matter to settle, let each person say their piece without being cut short, and go on until you find something all can accept. If there is nothing to settle, tell what you saw today, a story or a riddle. No screens.
practices.why: Maasai communities govern themselves by meeting. Men of an age-set gather under a tree, each may stand and speak holding his stick, and the spokesman draws the talk toward an agreement that all will keep. No one gives orders. In the evening, with the cattle safely in, grandmothers tell the children stories and riddles by the fire.
variations: Hold a household meeting in which everyone speaks once before anyone speaks twice.
Ask the oldest person you know for a story from their childhood.
Learn a riddle and try it on a child.

tasks.name: Read a chapter of The Worlds of a Maasai Warrior
Listen to Maasai call-and-response singing
tasks.meta: Listen · voices only, with the chorus keeping the rhythm in the throat

tasks.name: Look closely at a beaded collar
tasks.meta: Art · and learn what each colour stands for

tasks.name: Play a game of enkeshui
tasks.meta: Games · the Maasai form of the sowing game

tasks.name: Journal: who and what is in your care, and how are they?
Can land belong to one person?
Let someone older speak first, and hear them out
Drink a glass of milk slowly and think where it came from
Do one task together with the people of your own age
Listen to Maasai singing and follow the leader’s call
Wear something red today
tasks.meta: A colour of courage for many Maasai

tasks.name: Ask after someone’s family before any business
Drink a glass of milk or tea slowly, standing in the open air
Sit by a candle and tell the day as a story to someone
Name three people who depend on you and one you depend on

rules.why: Stop and ask after people and their families. Respect starts with a greeting.
Let them speak first and listen to the end. They have seen more seasons.

rules.text: Look after what is in your care
rules.why: Know each one. See to their needs before your own.
When a friend asks, give what you can and keep no account of it.
Share with your peers as equals. Nothing is done with one finger.
Let everyone speak, and stay until there is agreement.

read.title: The Worlds of a Maasai Warrior: An Autobiography
read.creator: Tepilit Ole Saitoti
read.why: From herding as a boy in Tanzania and initiation as a warrior to study in the United States and the return home. The best first-hand account in English.

read.title: Facing the Lion: Growing Up Maasai on the African Savanna
read.creator: Joseph Lemasolai Lekuton
read.why: A short memoir of a nomadic childhood in northern Kenya, boarding school and the long walk between them. Written for young readers and good for anyone.

read.title: Blossoms of the Savannah
read.creator: Henry R. ole Kulet
read.why: A novel by a Maasai writer about two sisters who return from town to their father’s country and resist what is planned for them.

read.title: Maasai
read.creator: Tepilit Ole Saitoti, with photographs by Carol Beckwith
read.why: The stages of life from birth to elderhood, described from inside and photographed with the families’ consent.

read.title: Being Maasai: Ethnicity and Identity in East Africa
read.creator: Edited by Thomas Spear and Richard Waller
read.why: Essays by historians and anthropologists showing how varied the Maasai are and how the image of them was made.

read.title: Oral Literature of the Maasai
read.creator: Naomi Kipury
read.why: Stories, proverbs, riddles and songs collected and translated by a Maasai scholar.

watch.title: Maasai Women
watch.creator: Melissa Llewelyn-Davies for Granada, Disappearing World
watch.why: Loita Maasai women talk about their own lives, marriages and work. Made by an anthropologist who spoke Maa.

watch.title: Milking the Rhino
watch.creator: David E. Simpson
watch.why: A Maasai community in Kenya turns from herding alone to running its own wildlife conservancy, and argues about the cost.

watch.title: Warriors
watch.creator: Barney Douglas
watch.why: Young Maasai men form a cricket team and use it to argue with their elders for an end to the cutting of girls.

watch.title: Enkipaata, Eunoto and Olng’esherr
watch.creator: UNESCO and the Government of Kenya
watch.why: A short film made with the community for the listing of the three male rites of passage as heritage in need of safeguarding.

listen.title: Songs of the ilmurran
listen.creator: Maasai warriors; many field recordings exist
listen.why: A leader sings a line and the group answers, while a deep rhythmic breathing in the throat carries the beat. There are no drums.

listen.title: Osiligi Maasai Warriors
listen.creator: A troupe from Kajiado County, Kenya
listen.why: Traditional songs and dances performed on tour to pay for a school and water in their own community.

listen.title: Maasai Hip Hop
listen.creator: X Plastaz
listen.why: A group from Arusha, Tanzania, who rap in Swahili and Maa over Maasai chant.

art.title: Beaded collars
art.creator: Maasai women
art.why: Flat discs of glass beads strung on wire, worn in layers. Red is for bravery and cattle, white for milk and peace, blue for the sky and rain, green for the land after rain.

art.title: The painted shield
art.creator: Maasai warriors
art.why: Buffalo hide stretched on a frame and painted in red, white and black with designs that showed a man’s section and age-set. One appears on the flag of Kenya.

art.title: The red cloth
art.creator: Worn by men and women
art.why: Checked or striped cotton in red, which is said to be the colour that lions fear. It replaced dressed hides in the twentieth century.

art.title: The milk gourd
art.creator: Maasai women
art.why: A long calabash with a leather cap and strap, often trimmed with beads and cowrie shells. Each member of a household has their own.

eat.title: Milk
eat.creator: Fresh or soured, from a gourd
eat.why: The staple. A family’s herd is managed so that there is milk through the year.

eat.title: Roast meat
eat.creator: Goat or beef, grilled on sticks beside the fire
eat.why: Eaten at celebrations and meat camps. Known across Kenya as nyama choma.

eat.title: Ugali
eat.creator: Stiff maize porridge
eat.why: Now the everyday food of most Maasai families, eaten with milk or greens.

eat.title: Soup with bark and roots
eat.creator: Meat broth boiled with medicinal plants
eat.why: Made at the meat camp, bitter and strengthening.

drink.title: Soured milk
drink.creator: Kule naoto
drink.why: Left to thicken in a smoked gourd, which gives it a taste of wood smoke.

drink.title: Chai
drink.creator: Tea boiled with milk and plenty of sugar

drink.title: Honey beer
drink.creator: Brewed from honey and water with the roots of an aloe
drink.why: Made for elders, and needed for blessings at ceremonies.

customs.title: The child’s greeting
customs.creator: A bowed head
customs.why: A child comes to an elder and lowers the head, and the elder touches it lightly with a hand.

customs.title: Blessing
customs.creator: Elders bless the young
customs.why: An elder blesses by sprinkling milk or honey beer from a tuft of grass, or with a light spray of spittle, which is a mark of goodwill.

customs.title: Grass for peace
customs.creator: A handful held up
customs.why: Grass feeds the cattle and is a sign of peace. A tuft tied to a gourd or held in the hand asks for a truce or a blessing.

customs.title: Building the house
customs.creator: Women’s work
customs.why: Women build, repair and own the houses, and can put one up in a matter of days.

games.title: Enkeshui
games.creator: Board game · Maasai
games.why: A sowing game of the mancala family, played by elders on a long wooden board with rows of hollows and seeds or pebbles.

games.title: The Maasai Olympics
games.creator: Athletics · Kenya
games.why: Warriors from the villages around Amboseli compete at running, spear and club throwing and the standing high jump. The elders set it up to take the place of lion hunting.

games.title: Riddles
games.creator: Word game · Maasai
games.why: Played in the evening between children and grandmothers, with a set opening exchange before each riddle.

games.title: Jumping
games.creator: Contest · Maasai
games.why: The high standing leap of the adumu is a test of strength and style among age-mates.

festivals.title: Eunoto
festivals.creator: Once for each age-set, about every fifteen years
festivals.why: The ceremony at which warriors become senior. Their mothers shave off their long hair. It belongs to the families concerned and is not a show.

festivals.title: Enkipaata
festivals.creator: Before a new age-set is opened
festivals.why: Boys travel their section together to announce the forming of a new age-set.

festivals.title: The Maasai Olympics
festivals.creator: Every second December, Kimana, Kenya
festivals.why: A public day of sport at the foot of Kilimanjaro, open to visitors.

festivals.title: Maa Cultural Festival
festivals.creator: November, Kenya
festivals.why: A gathering of the Maa-speaking communities of several counties, first held in the Maasai Mara in 2023.

places.title: Maasai Mara and its conservancies
places.creator: Narok County, Kenya
places.why: Grassland where Maasai families lease their land together as wildlife conservancies and go on herding. Stay in one that is owned by the community.

places.title: Amboseli
places.creator: Kajiado County, Kenya
places.why: Swamps and plains beneath Kilimanjaro, long used as dry-season grazing. The surrounding group ranches are Maasai land.

places.title: Ngorongoro
places.creator: Arusha Region, Tanzania
places.why: A great volcanic crater and highlands set aside in 1959 as a place for both wildlife and Maasai herders. Their right to stay is now disputed.

places.title: Ol Doinyo Lengai
places.creator: Near Lake Natron, Tanzania
places.why: The Mountain of God, an active volcano where people go to pray for rain and for children.

places.title: The Loita Forest
places.creator: Narok County, Kenya
places.why: The Forest of the Lost Child, a highland forest kept by the Loita Maasai and their ritual leaders. Go only with a local guide.

places.title: Il Ngwesi
places.creator: Laikipia County, Kenya
places.why: A lodge and conservancy owned and run since 1996 by a Maasai community.

ethics.title: Respect
ethics.text: Enkanyit. Give each person the honour due to their age and place.
ethics.practice: Show respect today to someone you usually take for granted.

ethics.title: Courage
ethics.text: A person must be able to stand firm and protect others.
ethics.practice: Do one thing you are afraid of for the sake of someone else.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: A guest is fed, and a friend in need is given what he asks.
ethics.practice: Give something today before you are thanked for it.

ethics.title: Solidarity
ethics.text: Age-mates share everything and no one eats alone.
ethics.practice: Share a meal with your peers.

ethics.title: Self-command
ethics.text: Do not show pain, anger or greed.

ethics.title: Stewardship
ethics.text: Cattle and land are held in trust for those who come after.
ethics.practice: Leave one thing in better condition than you found it.

philosophy.title: Wealth is what is alive
philosophy.text: A rich person is one with many cattle and many children. Both must be cared for daily and neither can be hoarded.
philosophy.practice: What is your wealth if you count only what is alive?

philosophy.title: Age as order
philosophy.text: Authority comes with age. Everyone will hold it in turn, and no one holds it early.
philosophy.practice: What will you be trusted with when you are older?

philosophy.title: The age-set
philosophy.text: Men who were initiated together are equals for life, whatever each later owns.
philosophy.practice: Who are your equals for life?

philosophy.title: Land in common
philosophy.text: Pasture belongs to the section. The herder uses it and moves on.
philosophy.practice: What do you use that you do not need to own?

philosophy.title: Giving without debt
philosophy.text: In osotua nothing is owed. Need alone is the claim.
philosophy.practice: Whose need has a claim on you?

philosophy.title: Black God and Red God
philosophy.text: One God sends both the rain and the drought.
philosophy.practice: How do you hold together what blesses you and what harms you?

philosophy.title: Agreement over command
philosophy.text: A leader speaks for his people and cannot order them.
philosophy.practice: Where do you give orders when you should be seeking agreement?

philosophy.title: Change and continuity
philosophy.text: Maasai have changed their customs before and are doing so now, on their own terms.
philosophy.practice: What would you change in order to keep what matters?

intro: The Maasai are a people of the high grasslands that run along the Great Rift Valley from central Kenya into northern Tanzania. They speak Maa, a language of the Nilotic family, and their own traditions and the evidence of language agree that their ancestors came south from the region of the upper Nile, reaching their present country in stages from about the fifteenth century. By the middle of the nineteenth century they held a territory some eleven hundred kilometres long. The census of Kenya in 2019 counted nearly 1.2 million Maasai, and there are perhaps as many again in Tanzania.

Their way of life is built on cattle. Traditional belief holds that Enkai, the one God, who is also the sky and the rain, let cattle down from heaven and gave them to the Maasai to keep. Milk is the daily food, with meat on occasions, and sheep and goats are kept as well. Because rain on the savanna is patchy, herders have always moved with the seasons, grazing one area and letting another rest. Land belonged to the section, not to individuals. Families live in a ring of houses inside a thorn fence, with the animals in the middle at night. The women build the houses.

Society is organised by age. Every fifteen years or so a new age-set is opened, and the boys initiated into it become warriors together, charged with protecting the herds and the community. They later graduate together into elderhood, when they marry, manage herds and take part in the councils where matters are settled by long discussion. Each age-set chooses a spokesman, who leads by persuasion. There have never been chiefs or kings. Ritual experts called iloibonok give advice and blessing. Women pass through their own stages, own their houses and the milk, and are known for beadwork whose colours all have meanings.

At the end of the nineteenth century disaster struck. Between 1883 and 1902 cattle lung disease, rinderpest, smallpox and drought killed most of the herds and a large part of the people. The Maasai call it the Emutai, the wiping out. British and German colonial rule arrived in the same years. By agreements of 1904 and 1911 the British moved the Maasai of Kenya off their best northern pastures to make room for settlers, and they lost more than half their land. Later, more was taken for the national parks and reserves that visitors know: the Serengeti, Amboseli, the Mara.

The pressure has continued since independence through farms, fences, the dividing of common land into private plots and, in Tanzania, removals for conservation and hunting areas. Maasai communities have answered in many ways. Some run their own wildlife conservancies. Many are Christian, most children go to school, and there are Maasai doctors, lawyers, novelists, members of parliament and athletes. Campaigners from within the community have worked to end the cutting of girls and early marriage, and to defend land rights in court.

The picture of the tall red-robed warrior with a spear is known around the world, and has been used to sell everything from safaris to cars, usually without asking. Real Maasai life is more varied than the picture and belongs to the people who live it.
This Onda takes its practices from everyday Maasai values and not from any ceremony: a proper greeting, walking the land, care for what depends on you, giving in need and talking things through.
guide.origin: The Great Rift Valley of southern Kenya and northern Tanzania
guide.era: Maa speakers moved south into the Rift Valley from about the fifteenth century. Around two million Maasai live there now

figures.name: Mbatian
figures.bio: The most influential oloiboni of the nineteenth century, who is said to have foretold the coming of disease and of white men. A peak of Mount Kenya bears his name.

figures.name: Olonana
figures.bio: Mbatian’s son, known to the British as Lenana. He was recognised by them as paramount chief, a post the Maasai had never had, and signed the agreement of 1904.

figures.name: Senteu
figures.bio: Olonana’s brother and rival for their father’s position. The war between their followers in the 1890s deepened the ruin of those years.

figures.name: Parsaloi ole Gilisho
figures.bio: Spokesman of the Purko warriors, who opposed the second move and in 1913 took the British government to court. The case was dismissed on a technicality.

figures.name: Edward Moringe Sokoine
figures.bio: A Maasai from Monduli who was twice prime minister of Tanzania, respected for his honesty. He died in a road accident.

figures.name: William ole Ntimama
figures.bio: A teacher who became the leading Maasai politician in Kenya for four decades and a fierce defender of Maasai land.

figures.name: Tepilit Ole Saitoti
figures.bio: Writer and naturalist from Tanzania whose books told the world about Maasai life from the inside.

figures.name: Henry R. ole Kulet
figures.bio: Kenyan novelist who wrote nine novels about Maasai society in a time of change.

figures.name: Kakenya Ntaiya
figures.bio: From Enoosaen in Kenya. She bargained with her father and her village elders to continue her schooling, earned a doctorate and came home to found a school for girls.

figures.name: Nice Nailantei Leng'ete
figures.bio: Ran away from the cut as a child and later persuaded the elders of her area to accept rites of passage for girls without it. Thousands of girls have gone through them.

figures.name: David Rudisha
figures.bio: From Kilgoris. Twice Olympic champion at 800 metres, he set the world record of 1 minute 40.91 seconds in London in 2012.

figures.name: Richard Turere
figures.bio: As a boy herding beside Nairobi National Park he built a system of flashing lights that keeps lions away from cattle pens at night. It is now used across Kenya.

history.detail: Maa-speaking herders move from the area north-west of Lake Turkana down the Rift Valley over several centuries.
Maasai sections spread across the plains of central Kenya and northern Tanzania, displacing or absorbing earlier herders.
Maasai country reaches from Laikipia in the north to the steppe south of Arusha. Wars are fought between sections over pasture.
Lung disease among cattle in 1883, rinderpest in 1891, smallpox in 1892 and years of drought. An Austrian traveller reported that two-thirds of the Maasai in the south had died.
His sons Olonana and Senteu fight over the succession through the worst of the famine.
Britain declares the East Africa Protectorate. The border with German East Africa cuts Maasai country in two.
The Maasai of the central Rift are moved into two reserves, north and south, which are promised to them for as long as they exist as a people.
The northern reserve on Laikipia is taken for settlers and some twenty thousand people and their herds are marched south at gunpoint. Many die on the way.
A national park is declared. In 1959 the Maasai living in it are moved to Ngorongoro on a promise that their rights there will come first.
Tanganyika and then Kenya become independent. The new governments press herders to settle.
Kenyan law gives groups of Maasai title to blocks of land. From the 1980s many are divided into private plots, and much is sold.
Landowners around the Mara and elsewhere pool their plots as conservancies that earn rent from tourism while grazing continues.
UNESCO lists three Maasai male rites of passage as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.
Tanzanian security forces move to fence off grazing land at Loliondo for a game reserve. People are injured and thousands flee. Relocation from Ngorongoro continues.

concepts.text: Living from herds on open range.
concepts.detail: A skilled way of using dry grassland that cannot be farmed. It depends on mobility, shared access to land and close knowledge of animals and plants.
Each man belongs for life to the set he was initiated with. Sets move together through the grades of warrior, junior elder, senior elder and retired elder, and each grade has its duties.

concepts.text: Respect as the basis of order.
concepts.detail: Without chiefs or police, order rests on trained respect: of young for old, of age-mates for each other, of hosts for guests.

concepts.text: Risk shared through bonds of need.
concepts.detail: Each herder keeps several such partners in different places. When drought or disease strikes one area, help comes from another.

concepts.text: One God of sky and rain.
concepts.detail: Prayed to at dawn and in every blessing, without temples or priests. Many Maasai are now Christian and use the same name for God.
The Maasai are a number of territorial sections with their own customs and dialects. They have never had a single government.
Grazing was open to all members of a section and managed by agreement among elders, with some areas kept in reserve for the dry season.
The blessing of an elder is sought at every step of life. His curse is feared, and the fear of it is the main sanction against wrongdoing.

concepts.text: Herds and wild animals on one land.
concepts.detail: Maasai did not hunt for food and their grazing kept the plains open. Most of East Africa’s great wildlife areas are former Maasai land.

facts.text: Many place names in Kenya and Tanzania are Maa. Nairobi comes from the words for the place of cool waters, and Serengeti from a word for an endless plain.
The flag of Kenya shows a Maasai shield and two spears.
Maasai traditionally did not eat wild game or birds, and did not dig the earth.
The English name of the Olduvai Gorge is a misheard form of oldupai, the Maa word for the wild sisal that grows there.
The Maa language has separate words for a great many cattle colours and patterns.

sensitivity.note: The Maasai are a living people with their own voices, and this Onda was written by outsiders from published sources. It borrows only everyday values such as greeting, care and sharing. It does not ask you to dress as a Maasai or to copy any ceremony, and it should be checked by Maasai readers.
requiredCaveats: Initiation and the other rites of passage belong to Maasai families and are not practices for anyone else.
The Maasai image and name are widely used in advertising and tourism without consent or payment. Buy beadwork from the women who make it and choose lodges owned by the community.
Customs differ between sections and between Kenya and Tanzania, and many Maasai live in towns, are Christian, or herd no cattle at all.

Some customs, including the cutting of girls and early marriage, are opposed and being changed by Maasai campaigners themselves. Spellings and translations of Maa words here follow English-language sources and may be imperfect.
